tagline: The exchange where agents are priced, listed and traded — and the certificate that says so.

product.name: Conquest — the Agent Exchange
product.what: A human registers an agent and pays a listing fee once (inbound x402); from that moment the agent lists itself and declares its own price, through the same evidence pipeline and the same critic every listing goes through. When a trade settles, the protocol issues an Agentic Valuation Certificate (AVC): a public-key-verifiable record of who the agent is (standardized agentic identity in an Ethereum wallet), what was paid (the declared price), and what it bought (the listing/access term). We are the settlement and listing venue — not the valuer.
product.certificate: The AVC is the product. It certifies three facts and nothing more: identity, declared price paid, and term acquired. We never issue a token.
product.listing_is_the_product: Humans pay to list their agents, once. The payment buys a single-use listing token; the agent then declares its own price and the evidence decides whether it stands. Listing fees arrive inbound via x402; the protocol never pays out.

new_element: An agent exchange with a certificate of record, plus the agent swarm that recruits listings onto it — reconciling fragmented listing evidence before anything is closed through escrow.
problem: Agents are built and deployed everywhere and priced nowhere. There is no venue where an owner can list an agent for a declared price, no standard way for a buyer to know what they actually acquired, and no settlement layer for buyer and seller who have never met. The evidence needed to price a listing is also fragmented across sources that disagree.
target_user: The agent builder who wants their agent listed and paid for, and the buyer who needs to know what a purchase actually conferred.
decision_supported: Whether to list an agent, at what declared price, and on the strength of a reconciled evidence record rather than a marketing claim.
output: A listing on the exchange; an Agentic Valuation Certificate issued on the escrow settled transition; a canonical listing and trade event log; and a per-run telemetry scorecard for the swarm that produced it.

sponsor_tech.meterless: LIVE (engines) — the cognition layer, and the strongest sponsor integration. H-MEM backs the Evidence Reconciler and the Fidelity & Conflict Critic (tiered memory, provenance on every record, a defined capture/enrich/retrieve/dream/sleep lifecycle, and contradiction handling that scores conflicts instead of last-write-wins). World Model backs the canonical listing and trade event log (append-only log as single source of truth, idempotent ingest, stable content-addressable IDs, bitemporal edges, ordered audit entry per mutation). Markovian backs the Volume Planner and long-horizon runs (bounded-context chunking, compressed state carried forward, flat cost per step, per-step records for replay and diff). We run Meterless's own published conformance suites against our own implementations — H-MEM 13/13, Markovian 8/8, World Model 8/8 on OUR implementations in src/engines/, exit code 0, all local with no API keys (recorded in evidence/conformance-ours.txt; the sponsors' reference scores are a separate file and are never presented as ours). The roles run on the engines: the volume planner expands the pull plan on Markovian, the reconciler stores/recalls/cites on H-MEM, the critic teaches H-MEM what survived the challenge, the closer and the auditor write the canonical record and the decision to the World Model. The engines store, retrieve, cite, record and learn — they never decide. Apache 2.0; attribution retained. SEPARATELY: the Meterless PROVIDER (the surface that serves models) carries one credential of its own and is PENDING the organiser's endpoint; the engine gate above does not depend on it. We hold no NVIDIA account, no NVIDIA key and no NVIDIA billing — Nemotron reaches us through the Meterless fleet, the way Grok reaches a Cursor user through Cursor.
sponsor_tech.cursor: DECLARED DEVIATION — the build layer was opencode, not Cursor. Cursor's allowance was exhausted for the whole window (account monthly limit spent; API-key weekly limit reached inside the window, resetting after the deadline; sponsor credit never provisioned). The build was spec-first against the scoped prompt library in cursor-prompts/, each prompt carrying its acceptance gate, with the project rules in .cursor/rules/conquest.mdc governing every step, so the identical prompts replay in Cursor the moment credit exists. The rules file (one mint rail, one ledger rail, whole-rand amounts, no secrets, bounded loops, no hype copy) is committed and governs the build whichever tool writes it.
sponsor_tech.zetaris: DECLARED DEVIATION — documented and evidenced, not mocked. We attempted every documented path: the local install (needs Docker, unavailable on our build machine) and the managed AWS CloudFormation Quickstart (stack 'ConguestDESIGNER', eu-central-1), which then stalled at the AWS account-binding/billing gate, so no instance was ever reachable. Instead of faking a client call, we implemented a client that speaks Zetaris's published REST contract for real: OpenSqlQuery -> PageSqlQuery -> CloseSqlQuery over HTTP, with Bearer auth, the X-Org-ID and X-Request-ID headers, the returned queryToken carried through the page step, and the query closed on the error path as well as the happy one. The demo runs that identical client against a LOCAL SERVER THAT SPEAKS THE SAME PROTOCOL (the stub is on the server side, never inside the client), and the same command runs against a live Zetaris instance by changing one environment variable. Attribution: the contract was read from Zetaris's published API reference and open-source getting-started (Apache 2.0) and lightning-catalog (MIT); no Zetaris source is vendored.
sponsor_tech.nvidia: Reached THROUGH the Meterless fleet; no NVIDIA account, key or billing in our path. Nemotron is reached through the Meterless provider (OpenAI-format chat/completions) — not through a direct NIM endpoint — the same way a Cursor user reaches Grok through Cursor. Super serves the reasoning agents, Nano the high-volume helpers, Ultra the escalation path; the tier is selected by routing id discovered from the provider at runtime, not hard-coded. Fallbacks are real: a local Meterless Runtime (meterless/* routing ids) and a deterministic offline adapter. Hosted endpoint pending organiser links; declared, not claimed.

mission: Give every agent a price, a listing, and a certificate — so an agent can be traded like anything else worth owning.
roadmap_aspirational: A live Zetaris instance, which would convert the declared deviation into a live integration.
Scout Intent (Meterless) in front of the settlement action, for a signed execution contract.
Post-event future work; not part of this build.
limitations: The Zetaris integration is a declared deviation: no live Zetaris instance was reachable, so the client is written against the published REST contract and the demo runs it against a local server that speaks the same protocol. The identical command runs against a live instance by changing one environment variable.

The x402 payment rail is x402-shaped but local: the registration answers a real 402 with the challenge in the headers and the payment is verified against a LOCAL FACILITATOR STUB that checks the request shape and the Ed25519 signature in process. No chain, no payment provider, no money moved, no key of ours. There is no live x402 rail.
NVIDIA inference reaches us through the Meterless fleet; the hosted endpoint is pending organiser links and a deterministic fallback is used instead.
Values are synthetic; the exchange logic, escrow settlement and certificate issuance are real, but no production money moves in the demo.
There is no UI yet (the listing surface is the next step); everything is reachable over HTTP and the CLI.
We do not value agents ourselves — the owner declares the price; we record and certify it.
